The trolley problem is strongest when it is not treated as arithmetic but as a conflict between two moral facts: five lives matter, and so does the prohibition on intentionally making an innocent person the instrument of rescue. In the switch case, diverting a runaway trolley from five workers onto a side track with one worker seems permissible because the one death is a foreseen side effect of redirecting a threat. In the footbridge case, pushing a person seems impermissible because the victim’s body is used as the means of stopping the trolley.

My resolution is a constrained deontological one: saving more lives matters greatly, but there is a moral distinction between redirecting an existing threat and intentionally using a person as a tool. Pulling the switch can be permissible; pushing the person is not.

The strongest objection is that this distinction may be morally cosmetic. In both cases, you knowingly choose a sequence of actions in which one person dies so five survive. If consequences and intentions are described carefully, “means” versus “side effect” can look like a rationalization for emotional discomfort.

My defense is partial, not absolute. The distinction protects a crucial social principle: people must not be treated as available material for others’ projects, even good ones. Still, the cases reveal genuine tension. Any resolution that ignores either aggregate human cost or inviolability of persons is too simple.
